summary: Argues that giving a computer a hostname and sharing it on every network compromises privacy, and discusses remedies such as fixing protocols or not disclosing the hostname.

plainLanguage.summary: Wearing a name tag everywhere you go tells strangers who you are. This says computers should stop.

questions: why is publishing my hostname harmful
why is hostname disclosure a privacy risk
subtitle: A privacy analysis of hostname disclosure in Internet protocols

tldr.problem: Computers transmit their static hostnames across networks, and many Internet protocols leak them unencrypted. An adversary can use a hostname combined with other information to identify and track a device and its user.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC analyzes which protocols expose hostnames (DHCP, DNS reverse lookup, mDNS, LLMNR, DNS-SD, and NetBIOS) and proposes replacing static hostnames with frequently changing randomized values when connecting to new networks.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is informational; it does not mandate changes but documents the privacy risks and sketches potential remedies, including randomized hostnames and protocol fixes.

facts.label: Protocol leakage mechanisms
facts.value: DHCP, DNS reverse lookup, mDNS, LLMNR, DNS-SD, NetBIOS

today: RFC 8117 is an Informational document published in March 2017. It does not mandate protocol changes or specific implementations, but documents privacy risks and proposes randomized hostnames as a potential remedy. The privacy concerns it raises remain relevant; implementations of hostname randomization have appeared in some operating systems, though not universally.

sections.title: Hostname Privacy and Identification
sections.content:
Computers have names, called hostnames, that are typically used for network administration and user identification. These names are part of the fully qualified domain name (FQDN) used in the Internet.

The RFC highlights a significant privacy problem: mobile devices transmit their hostnames as they move from one network to another. An adversary monitoring a network such as a public Wi-Fi hotspot can observe a device's hostname through passive monitoring or active probing. By correlating this hostname with other traffic analysis information, an adversary can identify the device owner and track their movements across networks.

The document illustrates this risk with a concrete example: if a laptop with the hostname "dthaler-laptop" connects to a network and also establishes a VPN to Microsoft's corporate network, an observer can correlate these two pieces of information to identify the user as a Microsoft employee.
sections.plainLanguage: Computers announce their names when they connect to networks, like wearing a visible name tag. If someone hears your computer's name and knows other things about you (like your workplace), they can figure out who you are.

sections.title: How Hostnames Are Assigned
sections.content:
Different systems assign hostnames in different ways. Consumer devices often receive names chosen by users, sometimes containing manufacturer suggestions that include device brand, model, or user information. Operating systems like Windows and Unix require hostnames for basic administration tasks such as remote login and file sharing.

Large organizations use structured naming schemes to ensure unique names across their networks. For example, within corporate environments, hostnames might be derived from an employee's login name, resulting in names like "huitema-test2."

Small devices like smartphones, which typically do not enable disk sharing or remote login, often receive manufacturer-assigned names. These range from generic names like "Windows Phone" to highly specific unique identifiers like "BrandX-123456-7890-abcdef", sometimes containing hints about the device owner's language or personal information.
sections.plainLanguage: Companies and people create hostname names in different ways: some pick simple names, some include their login name, and some use the manufacturer's code. No matter what, these names can reveal personal information.

sections.title: Protocols That Leak Hostnames
sections.content:
Many Internet protocols routinely expose hostnames when devices connect to or operate on a network. The RFC documents several major examples:

DHCP: When a device joins a network and requests an IP address using DHCP, it can disclose its hostname in the request. This traffic is broadcast on the network and easily observed.

DNS Reverse Lookups: DNS includes a mechanism for finding the hostname associated with an IP address using the "in-addr.arpa" (IPv4) or "ip6.arpa" (IPv6) domains. An adversary observing an IP address in use can query these services to retrieve the hostname.

Multicast DNS (mDNS): This protocol allows devices to advertise services and names using multicast queries over the local network. When a device joins a network, it announces its name to verify uniqueness. An adversary can monitor these announcements or send unicast queries to specific ports to discover hostnames.

Link-Local Multicast Name Resolution (LLMNR): This widely deployed protocol uses multicast to resolve names on local networks. Like mDNS, it allows adversaries to discover hostnames by monitoring announcements or sending queries.

DNS-Based Service Discovery (DNS-SD): This protocol helps devices discover services on a network. While service names are user-chosen, the protocol chain forces publication of the actual device hostname in SRV records pointing to service locations.

NetBIOS-over-TCP: This older protocol implements a name registration and resolution mechanism. Without a centralized server, NetBIOS relies on broadcast messages that easily leak resource names derived from hostnames.
sections.plainLanguage: When computers join networks or advertise services, many different protocols announce their hostnames out loud: DHCP shouts when asking for an address, mDNS and LLMNR call out to check if their name is already taken, DNS-SD reveals names when advertising services, and so on.

sections.title: Why Hostnames Identify People
sections.content:
A hostname alone may seem like weak identifying information, but combined with other data it becomes powerful. The RFC explains that hostnames serve as partial identifiers that narrow the search space dramatically.

Even generic-sounding names like "jupiter" or "rosebud" are chosen from vocabularies containing thousands of possibilities. Learning a specific hostname reduces the scope of potential owners significantly. When combined with other observable information, such as visited websites or network registries like LDAP or publicly available attendee lists (for example, at an IETF meeting), identification becomes straightforward.

Manufacturer-assigned unique identifiers like "BrandX-123456-7890-abcdef" are even more powerful. While they directly identify the device rather than the user, an adversary can correlate a stable, unique device identifier with a user through a single instance of cleartext traffic exposure or other side channels. Once linked, the adversary can track both the device and the user across multiple networks using just the hostname.
sections.plainLanguage: A computer name might seem like just a label, but it narrows down who you are. If someone knows your computer's name and can see other things about you (like which websites you visit), they can figure out your identity.

sections.title: Randomized Hostnames as a Remedy
sections.content:
The RFC proposes replacing static hostnames with randomized hostnames that change when a device connects to each new network. Instead of a permanent identifier, the operating system would choose a new random name for each network connection, announcing the random name in protocols like DHCP and mDNS.

This approach makes tracking difficult without preventing protocols from operating normally. Services like DNS-SD can still function; users simply cannot easily identify network shares by hostname anymore. The RFC notes that randomized names must be synchronized with other changing identifiers like MAC addresses and IP addresses to prevent correlation between the changing identifiers and the old static hostname.

Some operating systems already support per-network hostnames (such as Windows), while others maintain only a global hostname. For multihomed devices using a global hostname, changing it for each network creates challenges. However, the RFC suggests some operating systems already use different hostnames for different purposes, which could serve as a model for combining static and randomized hostnames based on their intended use and privacy implications.

The RFC emphasizes that further study is needed before widespread implementation of randomized hostnames. It also acknowledges potential impacts on security practices, such as incident response investigations that rely on hostname information to trace traffic sources.
sections.plainLanguage: The idea is to have computers pick a new fake name each time they join a network, instead of using the same name everywhere. This would make it much harder to track a device, but wouldn't break how services work.
